strengths: Addresses a clear and timely gap in MLLM evaluation for omnidirectional images with careful problem motivation
High-quality and comprehensive benchmark: 2,000 curated images, 4,000+ QA pairs, 10 well-designed tasks covering both general and spatial understanding
Rigorous benchmark construction with multiple human experts, cross-verification, and careful quality control to ensure reliability
Extensive evaluation of 20 leading MLLMs (proprietary and open-source) across both close-ended and open-ended settings
Insightful error analysis identifying three key failure modes (insufficient immersive cognition, options as hints, option anchoring bias) with concrete examples
Practical Omni-CoT framework showing consistent improvements, with notable gains on spatial-level tasks (+7.34% on egocentric view orientation)
Strong reproducibility effort including detailed methodology, released prompts, plans to release dataset/code, and explicit ethics/LLM statements
Clear and well-structured presentation with effective figures and tables illustrating key concepts
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty of Omni-CoT: viewpoint-guided answering and crop grounding are straightforward applications of existing techniques, with modest average improvements (e.g., +2.51% on open-ended tasks)
Relatively small benchmark scale (2,000 images) compared to recent vision-language benchmarks, potentially limiting statistical power for general conclusions
Open-ended evaluation relies on GPT-4o as automatic evaluator without human validation, introducing potential systematic bias; no inter-annotator agreement statistics reported
Incomplete architectural analysis: limited exploration of why different model architectures perform differently, and no comparison with alternative ODI preprocessing techniques
Scope limitations: only ERP-format ODIs evaluated; other representations (cubemap, spherical harmonics) not covered, reducing generalizability
Missing ablation studies on benchmark construction choices and alternative prompt designs; limited analysis of fundamental architectural limitations for ODI understanding
No statistical significance testing or confidence intervals reported, making it difficult to assess reliability of performance differences
Unclear generalization of Omni-CoT to future unseen models; framework development appears somewhat tailored to specific models studied

strengths: Addresses an important and underexplored gap in omnidirectional image understanding for MLLMs
Comprehensive benchmark with 2,000 high-quality images and 4,000+ QA pairs across 10 well-designed tasks
High-quality data collection with manual annotation by domain experts using VR headsets and rigorous verification
Extensive empirical evaluation of 20 leading MLLMs under both close-ended and open-ended settings
Detailed error case analysis identifying specific failure modes and limitations of current MLLMs
Good documentation of prompts, annotation protocols, and commitment to release data/code for reproducibility
weaknesses: Proposed Omni-CoT framework is incremental with limited novelty - consists of basic crop extraction, standard prompting, and re-prompting techniques
Modest and inconsistent improvements from Omni-CoT across models and tasks, with many gains within noise margins and no significance testing
Framework requires manual crop selection and multiple re-prompts, limiting practical applicability despite being 'training-free'
Approach uses ERP projection and cropping rather than truly leveraging native 360° representations
Shallow analysis of why MLLMs fundamentally struggle with omnidirectional understanding beyond surface-level error categorization
Large discrepancies between close-ended and open-ended evaluation results suggest evaluation methodology issues; open-ended scoring uses GPT-4o introducing potential bias
Benchmark size (2,000 images) is modest compared to recent vision benchmarks; limited diversity beyond indoor/outdoor scenes
No comparison with specialized methods or prior work in 360° image/video understanding
Lack of statistical rigor - no significance testing, confidence intervals, or analysis of whether improvements are meaningful
Unclear generalization of findings to other omnidirectional domains and content types

strengths: Addresses an important gap in MLLM evaluation for emerging omnidirectional image modality with practical applications
Comprehensive and well-designed benchmark with 2,000 images, 4,000+ QA pairs, and 10 diverse tasks covering both general and spatial-level understanding
Thorough evaluation of 20 representative MLLMs (proprietary and open-source) with both close-ended and open-ended settings
Clear insights about MLLM limitations: spatial understanding is substantially harder, and models fail to reason about immersive environments like humans do
Careful benchmark construction with rigorous annotation pipeline, human expert verification, and quality control
Training-free Omni-CoT framework is practical and immediately applicable to any MLLM
Excellent presentation with clear visualizations, well-motivated task definitions, and helpful concrete examples
Strong reproducibility effort with detailed prompts, construction procedures, code/dataset release commitment, and ethics statement
Detailed error case analysis provides actionable insights into failure modes and reasoning limitations
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty in Omni-CoT: multi-view crop extraction via inverse sphere projection and prompting refinement are relatively standard techniques without deep innovation
Modest performance improvements from Omni-CoT (often 1-3% gains in Tables 4-5) fail to close meaningful gaps in model performance
Incomplete ablation studies: Table 5 shows only full vs. component-wise comparison, lacks analysis of interactions between components or relative importance
Statistical rigor issues: no confidence intervals, variance estimates, or significance tests reported despite evaluating multiple models
Omni-CoT only evaluated on 3-4 models in closed-ended and 2-3 in open-ended settings, limiting generalization claims
Limited prompting baseline comparisons: only Zero-shot CoT is tested; missing comparisons with self-consistency, CoT variants, and other sophisticated strategies
Insufficient analysis of why Omni-CoT works or doesn't work—missing investigation of architectural limitations vs. prompting-based solutions
Uncertainty about generalization beyond the benchmark: no analysis of computational costs, failure modes, or performance on out-of-distribution ODI sources
Some tasks (OCR, basic attributes) may not be uniquely challenging for omnidirectional understanding versus regular challenging VQA
Using GPT-4o as evaluator for open-ended tasks (Section E.3) introduces potential bias; human evaluation would strengthen claims

strengths: Addresses important underexplored gap: Comprehensive benchmark for omnidirectional image understanding, filling a real need in the MLLM evaluation landscape with 2,000 high-quality images and 4,000+ QA pairs

High-quality benchmark construction: Rigorous methodology with careful image curation, multi-stage annotation (automatic + human refinement + domain expert verification), diverse indoor/outdoor scenes, and 10 well-designed fine-grained tasks

Comprehensive evaluation: Thorough assessment of 20 leading MLLMs with both close-ended and open-ended settings, revealing complementary insights and introducing dual-format evaluation as methodological contribution

Rigorous experimental methodology: Multiple runs demonstrating stability (Table 12), extensive ablations on Omni-CoT components, systematic error analysis identifying root causes (insufficient immersive cognition, option anchoring bias), and prompt sensitivity analysis

Strong reproducibility and transparency: Detailed construction methodology, all prompts provided in appendices, clear ethics and reproducibility statements, plans for dataset/code release, and documentation enabling reproduction

Practical training-free method: Omni-CoT demonstrates consistent improvements across diverse models (3-5% on spatial tasks) through viewpoint-guided answering, crop grounding, and response refinement without requiring model adaptation

Clear actionable insights: Identifies that spatial-level understanding is substantially harder than general-level (~20% gap), reveals how models fail to understand omnidirectional images naturally, and demonstrates option anchoring bias in closed-ended evaluation
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: Omni-CoT combines straightforward components (chain-of-thought, image cropping, response refinement) without novel algorithmic contributions; training-free approach is practical but represents lower technical bar than learning-based methods

Incomplete root cause analysis: While documenting model failures, paper lacks deep investigation into underlying causes and potential solutions; missing analysis of whether failure stems from training data, architecture, or inherent spatial reasoning limitations
Modest performance improvements: Omni-CoT gains are typically 3-5% on spatial-level tasks; unclear whether improvements justify increased computational cost of the pipeline

Dataset scope limitations: 2,000 images is moderate size; single source (Flickr) without geographic diversity analysis; only 10 task types without deeper task taxonomy; static images only without video 360° content

Methodological concerns: LLM-based evaluation for open-ended responses (GPT-4o) introduces potential bias; 'margin' parameter in Eq. 3 lacks justification; design choices (e.g., why 6 perspective views?) unexplained; some complex tasks (scene simulation) have unclear evaluation semantics

Missing baselines and comparisons: No engagement with specialized panoramic vision methods; multi-view baseline (Table 7) underspecified; no ablations on perspective view selection strategy or systematic comparison with classical 360° methods

Generalization questions unanswered: All images from single source (Flickr); no evaluation on diverse 360° image sources, synthetic environments, or video 360° content; unclear generalization of findings
Limited statistical rigor: Multiple runs shown (Table 12) but without confidence intervals, significance tests, or thorough statistical analysis; standard deviations small but not formally analyzed

Incomplete technical justification: ERP-to-cube-map projection described informally; why 6 specific views? No ablation on view selection; crop refinement mechanism (Section 5.1.2) seems critical but underdeveloped; mechanisms for why viewpoint-guided reasoning helps unexplained
